entry: Mobilized chair on two or more wheels, used when walking is difficult or impossible because of [[Injury|injury]], illness, [[Disability|disability]] or age-related conditions. Wheelchairs provide mobility, postural support and greater independence, and they come in many forms, including sports and beach models. The main distinction is between motorized wheelchairs, powered by batteries and [[Electric motor|electric motors]], and manual wheelchairs, which are propelled by the occupant or pushed by another person. In 1655 Stephan Farffler, a 22-year-old paraplegic watchmaker, built the world's first self-propelling chair, on a three-wheel chassis. The invalid carriage, or Bath chair, brought wheeled chairs into more common use from around 1760. In 1933 Harry C. Jennings Sr. and Herbert Everest, both mechanical engineers, introduced the first lightweight, steel, folding wheelchair; their "X-brace" design is still in common use.

American political party formed in opposition to [[Andrew Jackson]] in the 1830s. With the [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]], it was one of two major parties of the Second Party System. Whigs favored the American System: a protective tariff, federal subsidies for infrastructure and a national bank. They opposed [[Manifest destiny|manifest destiny]] and the [[Mexican–American War]]. Four Whig presidents were William Henry Harrison, John Tyler, Zachary Taylor and Millard Fillmore. Sectional divisions over slavery caused its collapse after the Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854. Northern Whigs largely joined the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]], which elected former Whig [[Abraham Lincoln]] president.

Interacting grand-design [[Spiral galaxy|spiral galaxy]] in the [[Constellation|constellation]] Canes Venatici, 31 million [[Light-year|light-years]] away. Also called Messier 51a or NGC 5194, it is 76,900 light-years in diameter and has a Seyfert 2 [[Active galactic nucleus|active galactic nucleus]]. It interacts with its companion, NGC 5195, and the pair is among the most famous and relatively close interacting systems, a favorite subject of galaxy interaction models. Charles Messier discovered it on October 13, 1773. William Parsons, 3rd Earl of Rosse, found its spiral structure with a 72-inch telescope, the first spiral "nebula" known to have one. [[Edwin Hubble|Edwin Hubble's]] observations of [[Cepheid variable|Cepheid variables]] in some spiral nebulae showed that they were separate galaxies. Amateur astronomers can see the pair with [[Binoculars|binoculars]].

Body of rotating water produced by opposing currents, or by a current running into an obstacle. Miniature whirlpools form in a draining bath or sink. More powerful ones in seas may be called maelstroms, and a whirlpool with a downdraft is a vortex. In narrow ocean [[Strait|straits]] with fast-flowing water, whirlpools are often caused by [[Tide|tides]]. Small whirlpools appear at river [[Rapids|rapids]] and downstream of weirs and dams, while large cataracts such as [[Niagara Falls]] produce strong ones. Many stories describe ships sucked into maelstroms, although only smaller craft are actually in danger.

Specialized sensory [[Hair|hairs]] that help most mammals sense their environment, also called *vibrissae*. Whiskers detect air currents and objects, aiding navigation, hunting and spatial awareness, and can trigger reflexes that protect the eyes. They also convey an animal's emotional state to other members of its species. Whiskers grow in clusters above the eyes, on the chin, on the forelegs, near the ears and above the upper lip. Most mammals have them, including all non-human [[Primate|primates]] and [[Marsupial|marsupials]], but [[Monotreme|monotremes]] lack them. Whiskers are stiffer, thicker and longer than body fur, with richly innervated follicles. Rapid whisking, a cyclic motion of the tips, can reach 25 Hz in mice. Similar structures occur in [[Insect|insects]], [[Arthropod|arthropods]], [[Crustacean|crustaceans]], fish and birds. It has been suggested that they evolved during the [[Triassic]] period.

Distilled [[Liquor|liquor]] made from fermented grain mash, usually [[Barley]], corn, [[Rye]] or [[Wheat]]. It is typically aged in charred white [[Oak|oak]] casks, and all classes share grain fermentation, distillation and aging in wooden casks. The name is an anglicization of the Gaelic word *uisce*, meaning "water"; the spelling whiskey is common in [[Ireland]] and the [[United States]]. Scotch whisky must be distilled and matured in oak casks in [[Scotland]] for at least three years. In the United States, bourbon must contain at least 51% corn in its mash. It is one of the world's most popular spirits, and Scotch exports were valued at £5.4 billion as of 2024.

Lightest [[Color|color]], achromatic, reflecting all visible wavelengths of light. It is the color of [[Snow|snow]], chalk and milk, and the opposite of [[Black|black]]. White pigments, especially [[Titanium dioxide|titanium dioxide]], produce it, while screens create it by mixing red, blue and green light. Priestesses in [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]] and [[Ancient Rome|ancient Rome]] wore white as a symbol of purity, and Romans wore white togas as symbols of citizenship. From the 18th century white became the most common color of new churches and government buildings, especially in the United States. Surveys in Europe and the United States associate white most often with perfection, honesty, cleanliness and neutrality. The [[Pope|pope]] has worn white since 1566, and white is the color of mourning in many Asian cultures.

Official residence and workplace of the [[President of the United States|president of the United States]] in [[Washington, D.C.]] It has housed every president since [[John Adams]] in 1800, when the national capital moved from [[Philadelphia]]. The Neoclassical design by Irish-born architect James Hoban was modeled on Leinster House in [[Dublin]]. British forces set the mansion ablaze in 1814, during the [[War of 1812]], and it was rebuilt. By 1948 its walls and beams were found close to failure, and [[Harry S. Truman]] oversaw a renovation that rebuilt the interior around a new steel frame.

River in North and East Africa, the longer but less voluminous of the two major tributaries of the [[Nile]], the other being the [[Blue Nile]]. Its name comes from the clay sediment carried in its water, which gives it a pale color. Strictly, the White Nile begins at Lake No, where the Bahr al Jabal and Bahr el Ghazal rivers meet; more broadly it includes the course from [[Lake Victoria]] to the Blue Nile. Its headwaters lie in [[Burundi]] and [[Rwanda]], and the most remote are 3,700 km (2,300 mi) from the Blue Nile. In [[Uganda]] it flows as the Victoria Nile to [[Lake Albert (Africa)|Lake Albert]], then as the Albert Nile to the border with [[South Sudan]], where it continues as the Mountain Nile, or Bahr al Jabal.

Man-made ship canal in northwestern Russia, linking the [[White Sea]] with [[Lake Onega]], which connects to the [[Baltic Sea]]. Opened on August 2, 1933, it is 227 km (141 mi) long, but its minimum depth of 3.5 m (11.5 ft) is inadequate for most seagoing vessels. The canal was built in twenty months by forced labor of [[Gulag]] inmates. Cost and time constraints of [[Joseph Stalin|Stalin's]] first five-year plan forced a shallower design than the 5.4 m (17.7 ft) originally proposed. Between 12,000 and 25,000 laborers died according to official records, while journalist Anne Applebaum estimates 25,000 deaths. As of 2008 it carried only ten to forty boats per day.

Southern inlet of the [[Barents Sea]] on the northwest coast of [[Russia]], bordered by Karelia to the west, the Kola Peninsula to the north and the Kanin Peninsula to the northeast. The whole sea is considered part of Russia's internal waters. The port of Arkhangelsk, on Dvina Bay, was for much of Russian history the main center of international maritime trade, conducted by the Pomors. In the modern era the sea became an important Soviet naval and submarine base. It is one of four seas named after colors, along with the Black, Red and Yellow seas. The [[White Sea–Baltic Canal]] links it with the [[Baltic Sea]], and its [[Tide|tidal]] amplitude rises from 1 meter in the south to 10 meters in Mezen Bay.

Leukocyte, or immune cell, of the [[Immune system|immune system]], which defends the body against [[Infection|infection]], other [[Disease|diseases]] and foreign entities. Unlike [[Red blood cell|red blood cells]], white blood cells have nuclei and are generally larger. They are produced from hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow and circulate through the [[Blood|blood]] and [[Lymphatic system|lymphatic system]]. The main types are granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils), lymphocytes (T cells and B cells) and monocytes. Neutrophils are the most abundant, at 50–70% of leukocytes. In the US the normal count is 4,000 to 11,000 cells per microliter of blood. An excess usually reflects [[Inflammation|inflammation]] or infection, while leukopenia, a count below normal, indicates a weakened immune system.

Very dense stellar remnant, with a mass comparable to the [[Sun]] packed into an Earth-sized volume. A white dwarf shines from residual [[Heat|heat]] and slow crystallization, not from [[Nuclear fusion|nuclear fusion]]. Stars like the Sun, too light to collapse into a [[Neutron star|neutron star]] or [[Black hole|black hole]], are expected to become white dwarfs. The Chandrasekhar limit, about 1.44 times the mass of the Sun, is the maximum mass for a non-rotating white dwarf; observed masses are largely between 0.5 and 0.7 [[Solar mass|solar masses]]. The nearest known is [[Sirius]] B, 8.6 light years away. The first recognized, 40 Eridani B, was identified as white in 1910, and the name was coined in 1922.

Hypothetical region of [[Spacetime|spacetime]] in [[General relativity|general relativity]] that cannot be entered from outside, although matter, energy, light and information can escape from it. It is the opposite of a [[Black hole|black hole]]. White holes appear in the theory of eternal black holes, as a region in the past of a black hole, but no physical process has been observed that could form one. [[Stephen Hawking|Stephen Hawking]] argued that a black hole in thermal equilibrium would time-reverse into a white hole, and others have proposed that supermassive black holes could spawn supermassive white holes.

Racial classification most often applied to people of [[Europe|European]] origin, and in a broader sense to anyone with light skin. The modern concept of a unified [[Race (human categorization)|White race]] entered the major European languages in the late 17th century, in the context of race-based [[Slavery|slavery]]. Before then, Europeans defined their identity by religion, ancestry, ethnicity or nationality. Greco-Roman ethnography occasionally described populations as white by skin color, but these societies had no concept of whiteness as a race. Contemporary anthropologists and other scientists regard a unified White race as a social construct with no scientific basis.

Largest living species of [[Rhinoceros|rhinoceros]], with a wide mouth adapted for [[Grazing|grazing]] and the most social of all rhinoceros species. The southern subspecies numbered an estimated 17,464 in the wild as of the end of 2023. The northern subspecies is critically endangered: as of 2018 only two were confirmed alive, both females held in captivity at Ol Pejeta. The last known male, Sudan, died in [[Kenya]] in March 2018. White rhinoceros can run up to 40 mph (64 km/h) in short bursts.

Belief that [[White people|white people]] are superior to people of other races, and the ideology that maintains white power and privilege. It has roots in the now-discredited doctrine of scientific racism and justified European colonialism. Its structures included the [[Atlantic slave trade|Atlantic slave trade]], the [[Scramble for Africa]], Jim Crow laws and [[Apartheid|apartheid]] in South Africa. Contemporary forms include white nationalism and [[Neo-Nazism|neo-Nazism]], and in the United States it is associated with the [[Ku Klux Klan]]. In critical race theory the term also describes a social system in which white people hold structural advantages despite formal legal equality.

Medium-sized [[Deer|deer]] native to North and South America, also called the whitetail or Virginia deer. It is the most widely distributed mainland [[Ungulate|ungulate]] [[Herbivore|herbivore]] in the Americas and, with its predator the [[Cougar|mountain lion]], one of the most widely distributed terrestrial mammal species. It inhabits everything from arid grasslands to the Amazon and Orinoco basins and the high [[Andes]]. In North America it is common east and south of the [[Rocky Mountains]] and extends north to the [[Yukon]]. Texas is home to by far the most, with an estimated population of 5.3 million.

Leucistic color morph of the [[Tiger|tiger]], typically the [[Bengal tiger]], with black stripes on otherwise white or near-white fur and blue eyes. Its pale coat results from a lack of red and yellow pheomelanin pigments. Natural occurrences are occasionally reported in India, but the last one seen in the wild was reportedly shot in 1958. Most white tigers result from intentional [[Inbreeding|inbreeding]] for entertainment, a practice the Association of Zoos and Aquariums bans for accredited institutions. Inbreeding causes health problems, including reduced [[Fertility|fertility]], weakened [[Immune system|immune systems]] and shortened lifespans.

[[Hemiptera|Hemipteran]] insects of the family Aleyrodidae, which typically feed on the undersides of plant [[Leaf|leaves]]. More than 1550 species have been described. Adults are 1 mm to 2 mm long, and many species are dusted with a floury wax, which gave the family its name. Their small size lets them pass through fine screens that keep out their natural enemies, so unchecked greenhouse populations can rapidly become overwhelming. Whiteflies excrete honeydew, which promotes sooty mold, and vector more than 200 plant viruses. Control relies on biological agents such as the parasitoid *Encarsia formosa*, along with cultural practices and [[Pesticide|pesticides]], though some species resist insecticides.

Capital and largest city of [[Yukon]], Canada, on both shores of the [[Yukon River]] in southern Yukon. It was incorporated in 1950 and is named after the White Horse Rapids, which resemble a white horse's mane. First Nations used the area for several thousand years. After gold was discovered in the Klondike in August 1896, prospectors arrived by steamship, and the White Pass and Yukon Route railway, completed in 1900, linked the city to Skagway. The 2021 census recorded 28,201 residents, about 70 percent of the territory's population.

American [[Organized crime|organized crime]] boss who led the Winter Hill Gang, an Irish mob group near [[Boston]]. The FBI said he informed on Italian-American [[American Mafia|Mafia]] rivals from 1975, which he denied. Tipped off about a racketeering indictment, he fled in 1994 and was at large for sixteen years, ranked second on the FBI's Ten Most Wanted list behind [[Osama bin Laden]]. He was captured in California in 2011. Convicted in 2013 of racketeering and involvement in eleven murders, he received two consecutive life sentences. Fellow inmates beat him to death within hours of transfer to a West Virginia prison.

American singer and actress, commonly called "the Voice", and one of the best-selling music artists of all time, with sales of more than 220 million records. Her self-titled debut [[Album|album]] (1985) remains the best-selling debut by a solo artist. She scored eleven number-one singles on the Billboard Hot 100 and starred opposite [[Kevin Costner]] in *The Bodyguard* (1992). Her drug use and marriage to Bobby Brown tarnished her image. She accidentally drowned in a hotel bathtub in Beverly Hills, California, with [[Coronary artery disease|heart disease]] and [[Cocaine|cocaine]] use as contributing factors.

1988 American fantasy comedy film directed by [[Robert Zemeckis|Robert Zemeckis]], combining live action and animation in a world where humans and cartoons coexist. [[Bob Hoskins|Bob Hoskins]] stars as Eddie Valiant, a private investigator who must clear the cartoon Roger Rabbit of murder. [[Walt Disney]] Studios bought the film rights to Gary K. Wolf's novel, and [[Steven Spielberg|Steven Spielberg]]'s Amblin Entertainment produced. The film grossed $351.5 million worldwide and won three [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]], including for Best Visual Effects. It spearheaded a renaissance in American animation and was selected for preservation by the [[Library of Congress]] in 2016.

American actor, comedian and television host, one of 28 entertainers to have won an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar and a Tony (the EGOT). She was nominated for the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Actress for *The Color Purple*, directed by [[Steven Spielberg]], and won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for *Ghost* (1990). She voiced the hyena Shenzi in *The Lion King* and played Guinan in *Star Trek: The Next Generation*. She has co-hosted the daytime talk show *The View* since 2007.
